description: I'm a student passionate about technology, AI, web development, and space exploration. I love experimenting with ideas and building creative projects. Through Cosmic Cartel, I want to bring forgotten NASA missions to life. Looking for teammates interested in design, 3D, animation, coding, space science, or storytelling. All I need is curiosity, creativity, and a passion to build!
summary:
ORBITAL CREW — Space Crewmates 3D

I built a complete 3D mission-simulator game in a single 774 KB HTML file. You command a four-person NASA crew aboard the Orion MPCV · Gateway Relay during one eight-minute launch window, with thirteen procedures spread across a three-deck, ten-room spacecraft. There is no mission-select screen: everything is live simultaneously, and your AI crewmates choose their own work like people on a real shift.

The challenge's core demand was interaction, so the procedures are five genuinely different hands-on consoles — a colour-matching wiring loom, pressure manifolds you trim into green bands, a launch keypad, Simon-style gyro memory, and a sweeping antenna alignment — each feeding a live progress bar and countdown.

Everything is procedural: the ship, props, astronauts and all sound are generated at runtime with Three.js and the Web Audio API. The only assets are public-domain NASA photographs, embedded as base64 — zero network calls at runtime.

It matters because it turns passive "click-to-progress" busywork into the actual motor-and-judgement skills of ops work, and proves a rich, offline-capable 3D experience can ship as one file.
details:
ORBITAL CREW — Space Crewmates 3D

Project Details

What it does and how it works

ORBITAL CREW is a first-person 3D mission simulator set aboard a fictional NASA spacecraft, the Orion MPCV · Gateway Relay. You play a flight engineer working a single eight-minute launch window with a four-person crew. Thirteen procedures must be signed off before the window closes; run out of time and the mission stands down.

There is no mission-select screen and no difficulty chooser. Every console is live on the same ship simultaneously, spread across three decks and ten rooms, so prioritisation and route planning are part of the challenge. Your AI crewmates work independently — they pick their own procedures, walk to them through the corridors, take breaks, chat to each other, and occasionally sit down to check their pads. Watching them is how you learn the ship's layout.

The procedures are not progress-bar padding. Each one is a distinct hands-on interaction: a wiring loom where you match colour-coded leads to their sockets; a fuel manifold you trim into green pressure bands before locking; a launch keypad where you read a six-digit flight code off a slip and key it in; a gyro sequence you memorise and repeat Simon-style across four escalating rounds; and an antenna alignment where you catch a sweeping needle inside a moving acquisition band. Every percentage shown on the HUD was earned by a real action.

The player moves through a fully modelled ship in third person — walking, jumping, orbiting the camera, sitting in chairs — and can open a live deck map to locate any procedure and drop a waypoint marker.

Benefits

  • Genuine skill, not grind. The five consoles exercise colour discrimination, pressure judgement, short-term memory, numeric accuracy and fine timing — the same motor-and-decision skills real console operators train.
  • Cooperative, not competitive. The "impostor" mechanic common to this genre was deliberately excluded; the design teaches teamwork and trust instead of paranoia.
  • Zero friction. It is one 776 KB HTML file. No installation, no engine, no account, no network connection at runtime. It runs on any laptop with a browser.
  • Immediately assessable. The eight-minute window makes it demo-friendly: a judge can experience the full loop, including success or failure, in one sitting.

Intended impact

The project is a proof that a rich, atmospheric 3D experience does not require a large team, a game engine or a distribution platform — it can be built in a browser, in one file, and shared as a link. For players, the intended impact is a shift in expectation: that a mission game should make you do the mission, not watch a meter fill. For the genre, it is a counter-example to the escalating scale of multiplayer social-deduction games, showing that depth can come from cooperation and simulation rather than betrayal.

Tools, languages and software

  • Three.js r128 — all 3D geometry, lighting, materials and animation
  • HTML5 Canvas / WebGL — real-time rendering
  • Vanilla JavaScript (ES6) — the entire game loop, crew AI, collision, minigame engines, state machine: no framework
  • Tailwind CSS (CDN) — HUD, menus, briefing screens
  • Web Audio API — every sound effect is synthesised live from oscillators and filtered noise; no audio files are shipped
  • Python — build pipeline that injects the embedded imagery and validates the output
  • Node.js — syntax validation of the bundled script
  • Playwright — automated QA, driving the game headlessly to verify every console, camera behaviour and win/lose path
  • NASA Image and Video Library API — public-domain mission photography
  • Git / GitHub / Vercel — version control and deployment

Hardware was deliberately modest: a standard consumer laptop. There is no server component and no GPU dependency beyond the browser's own WebGL context.

How it is creative

Everything visible is generated by code. There are no downloaded 3D models — the ship's hull, the consoles, the props, the chairs and the astronauts themselves are constructed from primitives at runtime. The crew members have articulated hip-knee-ankle rigs so their boots actually travel when they walk, and each is given a procedural personality (pace, diligence, chattiness, break frequency) so a shift never plays out the same way twice. The lounge chairs were modelled from a reference photograph: cream shell, glossy cantilever blade, wraparound wings and cyan light piping. Even the mission patch is drawn procedurally. The only external media are NASA photographs, embedded as base64 so the game works offline.

Factors we considered

  • Scope control. We resisted adding more consoles in favour of making five distinct ones — repetition would have undermined the interaction argument.
  • Tone. The genre's default is cartoon impostor styling. We chose a realistic, NASA-accurate aesthetic: correct suit detailing, meatball and flag patches, gold visors, clean industrial interiors.
  • Accessibility of difficulty. Three window presets (10:00 / 8:00 / 5:00) let a first-time player learn the ship and an experienced one chase the clock.
  • Performance. The scene is built once at load and kept under a strict draw-call and light budget, with frame-rate-independent damping so camera motion feels identical on fast and slow machines.
  • Offline viability and portability. Embedding assets rather than linking them means the file can be emailed, judged offline, and hosted anywhere as a static page.
  • Fail-safety. Automated tests drive every console to completion and every win/lose path, so a broken build cannot be shipped.
